larger_context_summary: Christian addresses Roxane during their courtship. Having tried to woo her without relying on Cyrano’s eloquence, he can produce only blunt repetitions of his love, while Roxane expects the refined verbal passion she associates with him. She does not know that Cyrano—who secretly loves her—has supplied much of Christian’s romantic language. The immediate stake is Christian’s ability to sustain Roxane’s attraction under his own identity; his sincerity is not necessarily in doubt, but his verbal inadequacy threatens the relationship.
interpretive_commentary: The line is a maximally explicit assertion of Christian’s present feeling, so its force is primarily truth-conditional: he presents “I love you” as a fact about himself. Although it is intended to advance a courtship and may affect the relationship, those consequences do not make the sentence performative in the narrower sense of undertaking a commitment or changing a social status by being spoken. Its brevity might sound emotionally intense, especially when repeated in the scene, but intensity alone is not evidence of reflexive or uncontrolled expression; Christian is deliberately trying to persuade Roxane. The play’s larger deception complicates reception rather than the line’s core semantics: Christian’s cultivated romantic persona depends on Cyrano’s words, yet this particular avowal is his own and appears sincere. Its dramatic interest lies in the mismatch between genuine feeling and inadequate expression.
